newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Debre slams proposed asylum law change.
newsitem.headline: France's Debre slams proposed asylum law change.

text.p: A leading French conservative said on Friday that proposed asylum law changes would open France's doors to all victims of Africa's many ethnic conflicts.
"These proposals are sympathetic and generous but totally utopian and dangerous," Gaullist former interior minister Jean-Louis Debre said.
Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Thursday took delivery of a government-commissioned report which proposed 130 changes to immigration and asylum laws.

One proposal, aimed particularly at victims of Islamic fundamentalist groups in Algeria, would extend the right to asylum in France to all victims of persecution, and no longer only those persecuted by governments,.

"Ethnic groups have fought one another throughout Africa for centuries," a clearly horrified Debre told Radio-Luxembourg. "If the law were changed, we would have to give asylum in France to all the persecuted African ethnic groups."

Debre was interior ministry from 1995 until earlier this year. He fathered increasingly stringent laws to curb illegal immigration which Jospin, before he became prime minister, indicated he would overturn.
But Debre said he was satisfied by the new proposals on immigration -- separate from the issue of asylum -- since they hardly changed the policies that he introduced.
A main left-wing magistrates' union said on Thursday the new proposals did little to relax Debre's laws.
Patrick Weil, the sociologist who led the team which drafted the report, told a news conference French policy would still be to prevent new waves of unqualified immigrants settling in France.

There are about five million foreign nationals in France, including about a million illegal residents. Most new arrivals are from Africa and Asia, and have more difficulty integrating than earlier generations of immigrants such as Spaniards, Italians or Poles.

The immigrants' difficulties and many French people's rejection of them at a time of high unemployment have fuelled the electoral rise of rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front, which wants to expel them.
Debre said the latest waves of immigrants did not want to become integrated into the French community or to learn French. "All they want from France are social benefits," he said.
